opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

The fundamental difference is the cost of being wrong. In the information world, if a large language model gives you a poor answer, writes a buggy paragraph, or hallucinates a fact, you can correct it, regenerate it, or ignore it. The error stays in the digital space. In the physical world, a car or a robot interacts with atoms, with people, with roads. One mistake can mean an accident or a loss of life. So the bar for safety and reliability is several orders of magnitude higher. Ninety-nine percent accuracy may be impressive for a chatbot, but for autonomous driving it's nowhere near enough. You need something like many nines, and that last part, the long tail, is where most of the difficulty lives.

Second, the physical world is open, continuous, and messy. Text, images, and code are already digitized and structured to some degree, and the internet gives us trillions of tokens to learn from. The physical world doesn't come with that kind of data for free. You have to collect it with sensors, cameras, lidar, radar, in all kinds of weather, lighting, and traffic conditions, across different cities and cultures. Then there are the corner cases: a child chasing a ball, construction zones, a plastic bag blowing across the road, unusual human gestures. They're rare, but they matter enormously, and they're hard to capture in data.

Third, it's a closed loop with real-time constraints. An information model can take a few seconds to think. A vehicle at highway speed has milliseconds to perceive, predict, plan, and act, and every action changes the environment, which then reacts back. You have to model not just objects but the intentions of other agents, pedestrians, drivers, cyclists. That's much harder than predicting the next word.

Fourth, there's the hardware and the system. In the digital world, you scale with compute and software and deploy to millions of users almost instantly. In the physical world, you need sensors, chips, actuators, vehicle platforms, maintenance, and supply chains. The cost structure is different and iteration is slower. You can't just push an update and see what happens.

And finally, there's society: regulation, liability, insurance, public trust. Who is responsible when a robotaxi makes a mistake? People are much less forgiving of a machine than of a human driver, even when the machine is statistically safer. Building that trust takes time and a very strong safety record.

That said, I'm optimistic. Large models, world models, simulation, and vehicle-road-cloud coordination are changing how we tackle these problems. We're moving from rule-based systems to end-to-end learning, and from information intelligence to physical intelligence and eventually biological intelligence. Autonomous driving will likely be the first large-scale deployment of embodied AI, and robotics will follow. It's harder, but it's also where AI will have its most profound impact on everyday life.

r001.rationale: It identifies drivers as other agents whose intentions a vehicle must model in the physical world, conveying interaction with human-driven traffic as a difficulty.

r002.rationale: It contrasts digitized information with the open, continuous physical world and says systems must model objects and other agents’ intentions.

r003.rationale: It describes varying weather, lighting, traffic, cities, and cultures, and explains that rare corner cases are hard to capture in data.

r004.rationale: It mentions large models and embodied AI, but does not distinguish foundation models’ knowledge from practical skills needed to act physically.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I've spent most of my career on the information side, at Microsoft Research, then at Baidu, and now the physical side at Tsinghua's AIR institute, so I've seen both up close.

In the information world, intelligence lives in a very forgiving environment. If a search engine ranks a result wrong, or a recommendation misses, or a language model gives a mediocre answer, the cost is small and the correction is cheap. You get the signal back in milliseconds, you have billions of interactions to learn from, and you can roll out a fix with a software update overnight. The data is abundant, the feedback loop is fast, and the consequences of being wrong are bounded.

The physical world is different in almost every one of those dimensions. First, the long tail. A car on the road or a robot in a home will encounter situations nobody anticipated, and the distribution of those rare events is enormous. You can drive millions of kilometers and still see something new on the next trip. In the information world you can tolerate ninety-nine percent accuracy. In the physical world, that last fraction of a percent is where people get hurt.

Second, the cost of a mistake is not reversible. A wrong click is undone with another click. A wrong steering decision at eighty kilometers an hour cannot be undone. So the safety bar is not "better than a human on average," it is orders of magnitude safer, and you have to prove it, to regulators and to the public, not just claim it.

Third, data is scarce and expensive. The internet gave us trillions of tokens for free. There is no internet of physical interaction. Every kilometer, every grasp, every manipulation has to be collected with real hardware, in real time, and often with real risk. Simulation helps, but the gap between simulation and reality is still a serious problem.

Fourth, you are dealing with a full stack, not just an algorithm. Sensors, chips, actuators, power, mechanical reliability, latency, cost. The model has to run on the vehicle with constrained compute and strict timing, and the hardware has to survive heat, rain, vibration, and years of use. Each layer brings its own failure modes, and they compound.

And finally, there is the human and institutional layer. Autonomous driving operates inside traffic law, insurance, liability, city infrastructure, and public trust. Those systems move at the speed of society, not the speed of software.

So I often say the information world was AI 1.0, and the physical world is where the real test comes. The large models have given us a tremendous foundation. But closing the gap between a very capable model and a system you would trust with your family in the back seat is the hardest engineering problem of this decade, and I think also the most meaningful one.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental difference is that, in the information world, you can often tolerate mistakes and correct them afterward. In the physical world, a mistake can have an immediate consequence. If an autonomous vehicle makes the wrong decision, you cannot simply undo it. So the requirements for safety and reliability are much higher.

And the physical world is an open environment. You have changing weather, unpredictable human behavior, and situations you may never have seen in training. The system has to perceive what is happening, predict what might happen next, and take action in real time. It is not enough to understand a scene; you have to interact with it safely.

There is also a very different data problem. On the internet, you have enormous amounts of text and images to learn from. For robotics, collecting data means operating machines in the real world. That is slower and more expensive. Simulation helps, but there is always a gap between the simulation and reality.

So intelligence is one part of the challenge. You also need sensors, control, hardware, and all of those components working together reliably. Getting an impressive demonstration is one milestone. Getting a system that works safely, day after day, across many different conditions—that is a much harder problem.

r004.rationale: It discusses data collection and system components, but does not distinguish foundation-model knowledge from practical skills for physical action.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental difference is that, in the information world, you are mostly dealing with bits. In autonomous driving and robotics, those bits have to become actions in the physical world, where mistakes can have immediate consequences.

A vehicle has to perceive its surroundings, predict what other people will do, and make decisions in real time, with incomplete information. And the world keeps changing. You have different weather, road conditions, and human behaviors. Something that works very well in one setting may fail in another.

There is also a difference in how you learn. In the digital world, you can run experiments quickly and at enormous scale. With a robot or a car, collecting experience takes time, costs money, and has to be done safely. Simulation helps, but it cannot capture every detail of reality.

So intelligence is only one part of the problem. You also need reliable hardware, control systems, and a way to demonstrate safety across a very wide range of situations. Getting an impressive demonstration is one milestone. Making it work reliably every day is a much harder one.
